findings.passage: As a kid he quietly asked classmates who was funniest and demanded reasons when it wasn't him, a story he told GQ in 2020 and again in 2026, and starting out he reported follower counts, not income.
findings.problem: GQ 2020 (reopened) has only the private wish: "I used to literally say in my mind in elementary school, 'I wanna be the funniest this year, I wanna be the funniest kid in the class.'" It has no polling of classmates and no demand for reasons; those appear only in DOAC 2026 (VTT 00:30:33-00:30:44). FAQ 1, the most-excerpted type answer, therefore claims cross-year repetition for the verdict-seeking behavior that decides Three over Eight, which is the overstatement future-01 asked to remove. The same mis-sourcing runs through the type section ("What tips the call is earlier verdict-seeking: the classroom poll...", C194, sourced only to S-GQ/S-RS24), FAQ 2, whose three deciding instances are all DOAC-2026 (C211), and the type_hypothesis discriminator ("the classroom 'who's the funniest' poll and demand for reasons (GQ 2020, C50; DOAC 2026, C80)").
findings.acceptance_test: FAQ 1 says GQ 2020 recorded his private wish to be the funniest and that the classroom poll and demand for reasons come from the 2026 interview. The type section no longer presents the poll as pre-promotional "earlier" evidence. FAQ 2 cites at least one pre-September-2026 instance that GQ, Rolling Stone or Billboard actually contains (for example "I'ma prove it to y'all," GQ 2020; "amazing that I can create my fan base," Rolling Stone 2024; "that kind of reach," Billboard 2025). C121, C194, C211 and the type_hypothesis discriminator and five-year deletion note are corrected, and medium confidence is re-justified on the corrected pre-2026 base.
